title: Ramadan: the new moon
hook: the month begins when the crescent is seen or the month is counted

segments.voice: Yesterday: salawat, blessings on the Prophet, one sent and ten returned. Your line was peace on him. Did you catch the little symbol, and read it? Day one hundred twenty.

It's the evening after the twenty-ninth day of the month before Ramadan. Just after sunset, on a hill outside a city, a small group of people stand facing west with binoculars, squinting at the sky where the sun just went down. In a family group chat, someone keeps asking: is it tomorrow? Has anyone seen it? Somewhere else, a committee is on the phone with people in three countries. Everyone's looking for the same thing: a thread of light, thinner than a fingernail clipping, low in the sky for a few minutes before it sets. Today: the new moon.
screen: `FACING WEST AFTER SUNSET.` → `IS IT TOMORROW?` → `A THREAD OF LIGHT.`

segments.voice: That thread of light is the hilal, the crescent: the first sliver of the new moon. The Islamic calendar is lunar. Each month begins with the hilal and lasts twenty-nine or thirty days. That's why Ramadan moves about eleven days earlier every year, as you heard on day six. The Qur'an, in Surah al-Baqarah, says people ask about the new moons, and answers that they are markers of time for people, and for the pilgrimage. So the sky is the calendar. A hadith in Bukhari gives the rule: fast when you see it, and stop fasting when you see it. And if it's hidden from you by clouds, complete the month as thirty days. Simple on a clear night in Medina. Harder for Muslims spread across every time zone. So Muslims today follow different approaches, and they're open about it. Some communities wait for a local sighting, with their own eyes, where they live. Some follow a sighting anywhere in the world, or in a particular country. Some use astronomical calculation to fix the dates ahead of time. That's why two mosques in the same city sometimes start Ramadan a day apart, and why the group chat is so busy. There's also a short prayer from the Prophet ﷺ for the moment the crescent is seen, reported in Tirmidhi: asking that the month come with blessing and faith, with safety and with islam, submission to God, and ending, speaking to the moon itself: my Lord and your Lord is Allah.
screen: `HILAL — THE FIRST SLIVER.` · `MARKERS OF TIME FOR PEOPLE.` · `FAST WHEN YOU SEE IT.` · `SIGHTING, OR COUNTING.` · then, large: `MY LORD AND YOUR LORD IS ALLAH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for the moon tonight. If you can, step outside, or to a window, after dark, and find it. Notice its shape: a sliver, a half, a full circle, or not there at all. Wherever it is in its month, it's counting days for someone. If it's too early, close your eyes now and picture that thin crescent low in the west just after sunset. Breathe slowly. If you pray, you can say the Prophet's words to it: my Lord and your Lord is Allah. The bell holds the time.
Hilal. The crescent of the new moon, the first sliver that begins every Islamic month, and Ramadan. Today's word.
Your line: watch for the crescent. Look up at the moon once tonight or tomorrow, and see where it is in its month. Whenever Ramadan comes for you, this is how it starts. Day one hundred twenty.

howItsDone: Muslims begin and end Ramadan by the new crescent moon: some communities wait for a local sighting, some follow a sighting elsewhere, and some use astronomical calculation, so start dates can differ by a day.

original.note: Arabic: the crescent of the new moon, which begins every month of the Islamic calendar.

trapdoor: what you thought: Ramadan starts on a date on the calendar.
what it means: the month begins with the hilal, the crescent, seen or counted.
what a scholar hears: 2:189 on new moons as markers of time; Bukhari 1909; and the modern debate over local sighting, global sighting and calculation.

sources.ref: Qur'an 2:189 (the new moons are markers of time for people and for the pilgrimage)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1909 (fast when you see it; if hidden, complete thirty)
Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3451 (the supplication on seeing the new moon)

notes: Hadith numbers cited from memory; please confirm. The Tirmidhi supplication is paraphrased, not a new prayer.
